{"title":"Nothing Gets Out Unescaped: A Run Through MarkupSafe","premise":"A web page wants to show a comment somebody posted: ``. Printed as-is into HTML, that string stops being text and starts being code — it is a cross-site scripting payload. MarkupSafe exists to make the difference between \"text\" and \"markup\" a property of the value itself, carried in its type, so that a template can mix trusted and untrusted pieces and the untrusted ones can only ever arrive as inert characters. This story follows that one untrusted comment from the moment it is handed to `escape()` until it comes back out of a rendered fragment as plain text again, and notes at each step exactly what is guaranteed, what is merely trusted, and who is responsible for which.","chapters":[{"n":1,"title":"The Trust Boundary: escape()","trace_lines":[2,5],"data_in":"s = '' — a plain str of unknown provenance","data_out":"Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:24-45","src/markupsafe/_native.py","src/markupsafe/_speedups.c:74-171"],"inputs":["''"],"characters":["escape","_escape_inner","_native._escape_inner","Markup"],"facts":["`escape` tests `type(s) is str`, not `isinstance`, so the fast path is taken only by exact `str`; the comment qualifies and skips the `__html__` check entirely (__init__.py:39-40).","The comment on lines 37-38 says `type(s)` is deliberate: a proxy object can lie about `__class__`, so `isinstance` would be a trust hole; `tests/test_escape.py::test_proxy` pins this.","`_escape_inner` replaces exactly five characters — `&`, `>`, `<`, `'`, `\"` — and nothing else (_native.py:1-8). Backtick, `=`, and whitespace are untouched; safety of attribute values therefore assumes the attribute is quoted.","`_native` replaces `&` first, before the four replacements that introduce `&`; reversing that order would double-escape every entity.","At import time the C version from `_speedups` is preferred and the pure-Python `_native` is the fallback (__init__.py:7-10). The C code escapes the same five characters for 1-, 2- and 4-byte strings and returns the *same object* when nothing needs escaping (_speedups.c:84-87).","The return type is always `Markup`, never bare `str` — the escaped text is now typed as safe."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q1.1","question":"The fast path only fires for an exact `str`. What happens when the caller hands `escape` a value that is already safe — does the text get escaped twice?"}],"answers":[]},{"n":2,"title":"The Unguarded Door: Markup() itself","trace_lines":[6,9],"data_in":"Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>') for repr; then the literal string '<script>...</script>' handed straight to Markup()","data_out":"\"Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')\" and a second, equal Markup built with no escaping at all","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:84-134","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:167-168"],"inputs":["Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')","'<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>'"],"characters":["Markup.__new__","Markup.__repr__","Markup.__html__"],"facts":["`Markup.__new__` performs no escaping whatsoever. It wraps whatever text it is given and declares it safe (__init__.py:122-131).","Before wrapping, `__new__` checks `hasattr(object, \"__html__\")` and calls it, so `Markup(obj)` of an HTML-aware object stores that object's own markup.","`__new__` accepts `encoding`/`errors` and only forwards them to `str.__new__` when `encoding is not None` — the bytes-decoding road, not taken here.","`__repr__` wraps `str.__repr__` in the class name, so a `Markup` is visually distinguishable from a `str` in logs and REPLs — a small but real safety affordance (__init__.py:167-168).","`Markup` sets `__slots__ = ()`, so instances carry no extra dict; the safety flag is the type, nothing more.","This is the project's one deliberate trust boundary in the other direction: calling `Markup(user_input)` is how an application gets a vulnerability, and the API cannot prevent it."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q2.1","question":"If `Markup()` will bless any string at all, what stops untrusted text from being wrapped — and who is accountable when it is?"}],"answers":[]},{"n":3,"title":"Idempotence: escaping something already safe","trace_lines":[10,17],"data_in":"s = Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')","data_out":"Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>') — byte-for-byte the same text","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:39-45","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:122-134"],"inputs":["Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')"],"characters":["escape","Markup.__html__","Markup.__new__"],"facts":["`Markup` is a `str` subclass, so `type(s) is str` is False and the fast path is skipped; the `hasattr(s, \"__html__\")` branch is taken instead (__init__.py:42-43).","`Markup.__html__` returns `self` unchanged (__init__.py:133-134), so the escaped text passes through untouched — escaping is idempotent for `Markup`.","The trace shows `__html__` called twice: once by `escape` and once again inside `Markup.__new__`, which re-checks `hasattr(object, \"__html__\")`. Harmless here because `__html__` is a pure identity, but it means a user-defined `__html__` with side effects or cost is invoked twice per `escape` call.","Had the value been a `str` subclass *without* `__html__` (e.g. `tests/test_escape.py::ReferenceStr`), the third branch `Markup(_escape_inner(str(s)))` would have run instead.","Guarantee established: `escape(escape(x)) == escape(x)` for anything escape returns."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q3.1","question":"Escaping a `Markup` returns a `Markup` — but what if an application subclasses `Markup`? Does the subclass survive a round trip through `escape`?"}],"answers":[{"id":"q1.1","answer":"Already-safe values take the `__html__` branch, which returns their text verbatim; the five replacements never run a second time, so no double-escaping occurs."}]},{"n":4,"title":"Delegated Trust: an object that writes its own HTML","trace_lines":[18,20],"data_in":"s = a User instance with id=3 and name='Alice \"The Great\"' (its own escape call elided in the trace)","data_out":"repr string: 'Markup(\\'Alice ...lt;b>Great</b>"\\')'","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:42-43","docs/html.rst:1-49"],"inputs":["User(3, 'Alice \"The Great\"')"],"characters":["escape","User.__html__","Markup.__new__"],"facts":["`escape` on a non-str object checks for `__html__` *before* falling back to `str(s)`; if the method exists, its return value is wrapped in `Markup` and never escaped (__init__.py:42-43).","Consequence: the result of `__html__` is trusted verbatim. The `User` class here is careful — it builds its span via `Markup(...).format(name)`, which escapes the name — but MarkupSafe has no way to check that an arbitrary `__html__` did so. `docs/html.rst:31-43` states this responsibility explicitly.","Exceptions raised inside `__html__` propagate out of `escape` rather than being swallowed; this was a historical segfault in the C path and is pinned by `tests/test_exception_custom_html.py`.","Only if an object has neither exact-`str` type nor `__html__` does `escape` do `_escape_inner(str(s))` — so `escape(None)` yields `Markup('None')`, which is why `escape_silent` exists as the None-aware alternative (__init__.py:48-61).","The surrounding `` markup survives unescaped while the name inside it is escaped — the mixed-trust pattern the whole library is built around."],"open_questions":[],"answers":[{"id":"q2.1","answer":"Nothing in the library stops it: both `Markup(text)` and a loose `__html__` implementation bless text unchecked. The guarantee is one-directional — escape() output is safe; Markup()/`__html__` input is the application author's responsibility, and the docs say so."}]},{"n":5,"title":"A Template That Escapes Its Arguments","trace_lines":[21,25],"data_in":"'

User: {user:link} said: {comment}

' wrapped as Markup; kwargs user=User(...), comment=Markup('<script>...')","data_out":"a Markup template plus a freshly constructed EscapeFormatter bound to Markup.escape (__init__ returns None)","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:313-323","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:332-338","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:154-165"],"inputs":["Markup('

User: {user:link} said: {comment}

')","user=User(3, 'Alice \"The Great\"')","comment=Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')"],"characters":["Markup.format","EscapeFormatter","Markup.escape (bound classmethod)","string.Formatter.vformat","_MarkupEscapeHelper"],"facts":["The *template* text is trusted (it is a `Markup`); only the substituted values get escaped. Calling `.format()` on an untrusted template string would not be protected by anything here.","`Markup.format` builds a fresh `EscapeFormatter(self.escape)` per call and hands off to `string.Formatter.vformat` (__init__.py:313-315) — standard-library parsing, custom field rendering.","Because the escape callable is `self.escape` (the bound classmethod of the actual class), subclasses of `Markup` format into their own type.","`format_map` is the same machinery with an empty args tuple (__init__.py:317-323).","Road not taken: the `%` operator (`__mod__`, __init__.py:154-165) wraps each argument in `_MarkupEscapeHelper`, which escapes lazily in `__str__`/`__repr__` and passes `__int__`/`__float__` through unescaped — a different path to the same guarantee, exercised by `tests/test_markupsafe.py::test_string_interpolation`.","`EscapeFormatter` declares `__slots__` but subclasses `string.Formatter`, which does not — so the slots save nothing; cosmetic, not a risk."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q5.1","question":"The field `{user:link}` carries a format spec. What decides whether `link` is handled by the object or by Python's normal formatting — and what happens if an object offers `__html__` but no spec handler?"}],"answers":[]},{"n":6,"title":"format_field: three doors, in order","trace_lines":[26,29],"data_in":"value = User(3, 'Alice \"The Great\"'), format_spec = 'link'","data_out":"control handed to User.__html_format__, which builds Markup('{}') and Markup('{0}')","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:339-354","docs/formatting.rst:10-52"],"inputs":["User(3, 'Alice \"The Great\"')","'link'"],"characters":["EscapeFormatter.format_field","User.__html_format__","Markup.__new__"],"facts":["`format_field` dispatches in a fixed order: `__html_format__` first, then `__html__`, then Python's default `super().format_field` (__init__.py:340-353).","Because `__html_format__` wins, the object receives the raw spec string `'link'` and decides what it means; MarkupSafe imposes no spec grammar.","Road not taken: if the object had `__html__` but no `__html_format__` *and* a non-empty spec was given, `format_field` raises `ValueError` with a message naming the type (__init__.py:343-348) rather than silently ignoring the spec.","Road not taken: `Markup.__html_format__` itself raises `ValueError(\"Unsupported format specification for Markup.\")` for any non-empty spec (__init__.py:325-329) — formatting a `Markup` with `{:>10}` is an error, not a pad.","In the default branch, the spec is coerced with `str(format_spec)` before delegating, so a `Markup` spec does not invoke the wrong `__format__` callbacks (__init__.py:351-353).","The whole dispatch is `hasattr`-based duck typing: any object claiming these method names is believed."],"open_questions":[],"answers":[{"id":"q5.1","answer":"`format_field` checks `__html_format__` first and passes the spec straight to it; an object with only `__html__` and a non-empty spec gets a ValueError naming the offending type, so specs are never silently dropped."}]},{"n":7,"title":"The Innermost Escape: the user's name","trace_lines":[30,44],"data_in":"Markup('{0}').format('Alice \"The Great\"')","data_out":"Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:339-354","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:230-240","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:24-45"],"inputs":["'Alice \"The Great\"'","format_spec = ''"],"characters":["Markup.format","EscapeFormatter.format_field","Markup.escape","escape","Markup.__new__"],"facts":["The name is a plain `str` with no `__html__`, so it reaches the third branch: `super().format_field(value, str(''))` and then `str(self.escape(rv))` (__init__.py:350-354).","Escaping converts `\"` to `"` and ``/`` to `<b>`/`</b>`: the double quote matters because the name lands next to quoted attribute values elsewhere in the page.","`format_field` returns a plain `str`, not a `Markup` — `str(self.escape(rv))` deliberately strips the type, because `string.Formatter.vformat` concatenates fields with plain string operations.","Even an escaped field passes through `escape` only once; `escape` is called on the *rendered* field, so numbers, dates and anything else formatted by Python's default machinery are escaped too (`tests/test_markupsafe.py::test_formatting_with_objects`).","The inner `Markup('{}').format(...)` seen earlier runs the same path twice more (trace line 44, elided): once for `self.id` (an int, escaped harmlessly) and once for the already-safe span."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q7.1","question":"`format_field` hands back a bare `str`, losing the safe type. Does the final result still come out as `Markup`, or has the guarantee leaked away mid-render?"}],"answers":[]},{"n":8,"title":"Markup.escape: the type-preserving wrapper","trace_lines":[45,55],"data_in":"s = Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')","data_out":"'Alice "The <b>Great</b>"' as a plain str, unchanged","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:230-240","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:39-45","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:133-134"],"inputs":["Markup('...')"],"characters":["Markup.escape","escape","Markup.__html__","Markup.__new__"],"facts":["`Markup.escape` is a classmethod that calls the module-level `escape` and then, only if `rv.__class__ is not cls`, re-wraps the result in `cls` (__init__.py:235-240) — so a `Markup` subclass gets its own type back.","Here the value returned by `User.__html_format__` is already a `Markup`, so the run takes the `__html__` path and the markup survives verbatim: the `` and `` tags are not escaped while the name inside them stays escaped.","This is the second place idempotence pays off: a value can pass through escaping any number of nested templates without its entities being re-escaped.","The common case (`rv.__class__ is cls`) returns the object `escape` built rather than constructing another — one allocation saved on the hot path.","The trace shows the familiar double `__html__` call (once in `escape`, once in `Markup.__new__`) for every nested field."],"open_questions":[],"answers":[{"id":"q3.1","answer":"Yes: `Markup.escape` compares `rv.__class__` with `cls` and re-wraps when they differ, so escaping, formatting, joining and concatenation on a `Markup` subclass all return that subclass."}]},{"n":9,"title":"Reassembly: the page becomes Markup again","trace_lines":[56,61],"data_in":"the remaining field `{comment}` = Markup('<script>...</script>'), plus the rendered pieces","data_out":"Markup('

User: Alice "The <b>Great</b>" said: <script>alert(document.cookie);</script>

')","code":["src/markupsafe/__init__.py:313-315","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:339-354","src/markupsafe/__init__.py:122-131"],"inputs":["Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')"],"characters":["EscapeFormatter.format_field","string.Formatter.vformat","Markup.format","Markup.__new__","Markup.__repr__"],"facts":["The `{comment}` field (trace line 56, told once already) takes the `__html__` branch of `format_field`, so the pre-escaped comment is inserted without a second round of escaping.","`vformat` joins the trusted literal template text with the escaped field strings into one plain `str`; `Markup.format` then wraps that whole string with `self.__class__(...)` (__init__.py:315).","That final wrap is where the type-level guarantee is restored: every substituted field passed through `escape`, and the only unescaped text is the template the application wrote itself.","The resulting fragment contains `<script>` and never `', then + Markup('')","data_out":"Markup('
</p> & <script>oops</script>

')"],"characters":["Markup.__add__","Markup.escape","escape","Markup.__new__","Markup.__repr__"],"facts":["`Markup.__add__` escapes its right operand with `self.escape(value)` and wraps the concatenation in `self.__class__` (__init__.py:136-140) — so `safe + untrusted` is safe, which is the single most common real-world use after `escape` itself.","The second `+` has a `Markup` on the right; it goes through the same `Markup.escape` call and comes back unchanged, so safe + safe does not double-escape.","`__add__` guards with `isinstance(value, str) or hasattr(value, \"__html__\")` and returns `NotImplemented` otherwise; Python then raises `TypeError`. Adding an int to a `Markup` fails loudly rather than stringifying it.","`__radd__` mirrors this for `plain + markup`, escaping the left operand first (__init__.py:142-146), so direction does not matter.","The same wrap-and-escape pattern covers the rest of the `str` API: `join` escapes every element, `replace` escapes only its `new` argument, and `ljust`/`rjust`/`center` escape the fill character, while `strip`, `lstrip`, `rstrip`, `removeprefix`/`removesuffix` and `partition` deliberately do *not* escape their arguments (CHANGES.rst 3.0.0) because they are search operations, not insertion.","`split`, `rsplit`, `splitlines`, `partition` and `__getitem__` return `Markup` pieces — slicing safe markup can still split an entity in half, producing well-typed but malformed output. A real sharp edge, accepted by design."],"open_questions":[{"id":"q10.1","question":"Everything so far has only added safety. Is there any operation here that hands back text that is *not* safe — and would the type still say so?"}],"answers":[]},{"n":11,"title":"striptags: the exit back to plain text","trace_lines":[92,99],"data_in":"the page Markup('
